question.title: Digital access to museum collections
question.text: Museums increasingly make their collections available online, but digital access is not simply a matter of uploading photographs. A useful digital record needs context. Visitors may need to know where an object was made, how it was used and why different communities value it. Accurate descriptions make collections searchable and help prevent misleading interpretations. Online access can benefit people who live far from a museum or cannot enter the building easily. It can also support teachers who want to compare objects from several institutions. Nevertheless, a photograph cannot reproduce every aspect of a physical object. Its scale, texture and surrounding exhibition may be difficult to convey. Digital projects also require continuing maintenance. Websites, file formats and accessibility requirements change, so institutions must budget for future updates. The strongest approach treats digital collections as a complement to physical visits, not a complete replacement. Technology is most useful when it broadens access while preserving the context that gives an object meaning.

question.title: Reducing food waste on campus
question.text: A university cafeteria that wants to reduce food waste should first find out where the waste occurs. Food discarded during preparation requires a different response from food left on customers’ plates. For example, better forecasting may prevent the kitchen from preparing too many portions, while allowing customers to choose a smaller serving may reduce plate waste. Staff should measure waste over several ordinary weeks rather than draw conclusions from one unusually busy day. The results can guide a small trial, such as changing portion sizes at one counter. Importantly, reducing waste does not mean ignoring food safety. Surplus food can only be redistributed when storage, handling and collection meet the relevant requirements. Communication also matters: customers may accept changes more readily if they understand the reasons and retain a choice of portions. Finally, the cafeteria should measure waste again after the trial. A successful programme uses evidence, tests practical changes and checks whether those changes actually produce a lasting improvement.

Forecasting reduces overproduction; portion choices can reduce plate waste.
Collect representative data and trial a targeted change.
Redistribution must still satisfy food-safety requirements.

question.title: Extending library opening hours
turns: Maya

I think the library should stay open later throughout the semester, not only during exams. Some students work in the evening and need somewhere quiet afterwards. My shared house is noisy, so having access until midnight would make a real difference. What do you both think?
Ben

I understand the need, but opening the whole building could be expensive. We would need security, lighting and staff even if only a few students came. I would rather see a limited late-opening area, with student-card access, than promise a service the library cannot sustain.
Clara

A small area sounds sensible, but getting home safely is another issue. The last bus leaves before midnight. Students without cars might not benefit unless transport is considered too. Perhaps the university could coordinate a shuttle on the busiest nights rather than run it every evening.
Maya

That is a fair point. I do not need the borrowing desk to stay open; I mainly need a desk, power and internet. We could start with the ground-floor study room. A short survey might tell us which nights working students actually need it most.
Ben

I would support a trial based on that survey. We could count visits and check the cost for six weeks, then decide whether to continue. Clear rules would matter, especially about noise, visitors and what students should do if they need help after staff leave.
Clara

Then our recommendation could combine a small supervised study area with a transport check. We should ask students about both demand and travel, and make sure accessibility is included. That gives the university evidence before it commits to opening the entire library later.

question.title: Choosing a group-project format
turns: Daniel

For our environmental project, I would like to make a short video instead of a slide presentation. We could show the recycling facilities around campus and interview students. That might make our findings easier to understand than reading statistics from a screen during the final class.
Leah

A video could be engaging, but editing takes time and none of us has much experience. We also have to show how we collected and analysed our data. I worry that production work might distract us from the research, which is the main part of the assessment.
Omar

Could we combine the approaches? A few short clips could introduce the problem, followed by slides explaining the evidence. We should also provide captions and avoid filming anyone without permission. The format should help communicate the findings rather than become the main focus of the project.
Daniel

I like that compromise. We could record the facilities without identifying students, and use an anonymous questionnaire instead of interviews. I can take responsibility for two brief clips. If the clips do not work well, the research presentation would still be complete without them.
Leah

That makes the workload more manageable. Let us agree on the research questions and divide the analysis first. Then we can set a strict time limit for filming and editing. I would also like us to practise together so the final presentation feels like one coherent explanation.
Omar

Agreed. We should check the assessment instructions before committing, share a draft early and keep the clips short and accessible. The final plan is a slide-based presentation supported by video, with research quality, consent and clear teamwork taking priority over elaborate production.

question.title: Learning from a prototype
question.text:
A prototype is an early version of a product or service used to explore how an idea might work. It may be a rough model, a simple digital screen or even a role-play of a proposed service. Its purpose is not to impress an audience with a finished result. Instead, it allows a team to test important assumptions before committing substantial resources.

The value of a prototype depends on the question it helps answer. A detailed model can be wasteful if the team only needs to check whether people understand a basic instruction. Conversely, an attractive sketch cannot establish whether a physical mechanism will operate safely. Teams therefore need to choose a level of detail that suits the uncertainty they are investigating.

Feedback also requires interpretation. Participants may say that they like a design while struggling to use it, so observing their actions can reveal difficulties that a simple preference survey misses. A disappointing trial can still be useful when it exposes a weakness early enough to change the proposal.

Prototyping is consequently a process of learning rather than a single demonstration. Teams build an appropriate model, gather relevant evidence and revise their assumptions. By repeating this cycle, they can reduce uncertainty and direct their effort towards solutions that address a real need.
keyPoints: Prototypes test assumptions before substantial resources are committed.
The model and evaluation method should match the uncertainty being investigated.
Observation, feedback and repeated revision make prototyping a learning process.
question.sample: Prototypes help teams test assumptions before committing substantial resources, and their level of detail and evaluation methods should match the uncertainty being investigated; by observing use, interpreting feedback and revising their ideas repeatedly, teams can reduce uncertainty and develop solutions that address a real need.

question.title: Managing a seed collection
question.text:
Seed collections can help protect plant diversity by keeping material that may otherwise disappear from farms or natural habitats. However, placing seeds in storage is only the beginning of conservation. The collection must retain information about where each sample came from, when it was gathered and the conditions in which the parent plants grew. Without these records, researchers may struggle to interpret the differences between samples or choose material suitable for a future purpose.

Stored seeds also change over time. Their ability to germinate can decline, even under carefully controlled conditions. Staff therefore test samples periodically and produce replacement seed when necessary. This process needs care because growing only a small number of plants may unintentionally narrow the genetic variety that the original sample contained.

Decisions about access create further responsibilities. Farmers and local communities may have maintained valuable varieties for generations. Institutions need clear arrangements that recognise those contributions and explain how material and associated knowledge will be used.

A useful seed collection is thus an active system rather than a permanent warehouse. question.title: Practical projects at university
question.text: Some universities require every student to complete a practical project with a local organisation as part of their degree. Discuss one benefit and one difficulty of this requirement, and explain whether you support making it compulsory.

Develop one relevant difficulty of the requirement.

question.sample:
A practical project with a local organisation can connect university study with problems outside the classroom. Although such projects can offer valuable experience, requiring every student to participate creates difficulties that universities must address. I support a compulsory project only when students receive suitable choices and support.

One benefit is the opportunity to apply knowledge in a setting where the answer is not supplied in a textbook. For example, a group studying communication might help a community centre improve information for new visitors. Students would need to understand the audience, discuss competing priorities and revise their work after feedback. This process can strengthen judgement as well as subject knowledge.

A difficulty is that external projects can place unequal demands on students. Someone with a job or caring responsibilities may be unable to attend meetings during ordinary working hours. An organisation may also change its plans unexpectedly, leaving students dependent on circumstances beyond their control. A compulsory requirement would be unfair if these problems affected access to assessment.

Universities should therefore offer several project formats, including options that can be completed remotely or within a predictable timetable. They should assess the student’s contribution and learning rather than the organisation’s eventual success. With these arrangements, a practical project can be a valuable part of every degree. Without them, participation should remain optional rather than becoming a barrier to completion.

question.text: When a town installs public benches, it may report success by counting how many seats have been added.
